title: How the course works
text:
By the end of the course, you should be able to:

Situate your own research interest within the 70-year trajectory of the CEM field and explain why your question is legitimate research now.
Construct and defend a complete horseshoe for your own study — from an observed problem in practice through to a claimed contribution to knowledge and its practical significance.
Diagnose a research problem and state a question that is answerable, non-trivial, and matched to an appropriate design (methodological fit).
Reverse-engineer any empirical CEM paper: identify its claim, its inferential logic, its threats to validity, and what would falsify it.
Execute small-scale instances of six different methods (review, coding, survey, modeling, experiment design, reproduction).
Write and defend a proposal that would survive a real review panel, and write a competent referee report on someone else’s.
Apply research ethics and IRB requirements to your own proposed study.

Course mechanics

4.1 Weekly roles (rotating)
Roles run in W4, W5, W6, W7 and W9–W14 (ten weeks). W1–W3 are framing weeks with their own formats (§5); W8 and W15 are presentation/defense days with no role rotation.
Ten weeks × 7 slots = 70 slots for 16 students, so you’ll get roughly four turns: each of the four roles at least once, with any fifth turn falling in the week closest to your own topic. A three-choice preference list is collected in Week 1 and the fixed roster is published in Week 3, alongside the horseshoe assignment. One backup per week is designated so an absence doesn’t collapse the session.

4.3 If the course meets 2 × 75 min
Session A = framing + Method Leads + Exemplar Analysts + Skeptics. Session B = discussion + lab + synthesis. Labs then need to be sized to 45 minutes.


4.4 The Horseshoe Wall
Your horseshoe, built in W3, is posted on the course site and revised weekly. After each method week, update the Research Tasks box if that week gave you a better instrument, or the Theoretical Limitation box if it gave you a better argument. The W7 pre-proposal is a prose expansion of your wall entry.


4.5 Tools
R/RStudio or Python; Zotero; Taguette or NVivo/ATLAS.ti; VOSviewer; G*Power or the pwr package; lavaan and seminr (or SmartPLS); Simphony/AnyLogic or SimPy; OSF for preregistration. All lab datasets are provided; you don’t need to collect your own data for a lab.


4.6 How research ethics is handled
Research ethics doesn’t map well onto the Method Lead / Exemplar Analyst / Skeptic format — there’s no single paper to reverse-engineer the way there is for a method, and the useful skill (writing a correct protocol) benefits from direct instruction more than adversarial debate. It’s handled in three small, well-timed touchpoints instead:

Pre-course module (assigned Week 1, due before Week 4). Read the Belmont Report (12 pp.) and Munafò et al. (2017), “A manifesto for reproducible science,” and review the SNU IRB submission process. No seminar time is spent; completion is checked with a two-question reflection submitted online (credit/no-credit).
A 15-minute briefing in Week 4’s framing segment. What a defensible protocol looks like for construction research specifically — site access, vulnerable populations (migrant labor, as in the Tutt et al. reading), and physical risk for sensor/XR studies. You leave with the assignment: draft the IRB protocol section for your own horseshoe study, due at the start of Week 5.
A 10-minute Q&A at the open of Week 5, before the qualitative-interviewing content begins, addressing common problems in the submitted drafts. The drafts themselves aren’t separately graded as a lab — they feed directly into the “Ethics, feasibility, and timeline” line of the final proposal rubric (§7.3).

If your program’s IRB office requires a certified training module (e.g., CITI training) before you can submit protocols, that sits alongside item 1 above.

How the course runs
This is a seminar, not a lecture course. Most weeks, four of you are in an assigned role — Method Lead, Exemplar Analyst, Skeptic, or Discussant — and everyone else has submitted a question in advance. The instructor frames the method at the start of class and ties it together at the end; the middle is yours.
Two things anchor the whole semester: the history of the field (Week 2) and the CIFE horseshoe research process (Week 3), which you will use to structure your own proposal from Week 3 through the final defense in Week 15.
If you are not sure what your role actually requires, read the Week 5 role walkthrough — it follows one week end to end with worked examples of every deliverable.

A note on citations
All readings listed here are real and widely used. A few items from the ASCE Second Special Collection on Research Methodologies in CEM (JCEM, 2022–2023) and the original 2010 JCEM special issue are methodological discussion or position papers rather than empirical studies — these are labeled “CEM methods reading,” not “exemplar,” throughout. The distinction matters when you are assigned as Exemplar Analyst: you cannot reverse-engineer a study design out of an essay about study design.

title: Week 5 — How the seminar actually works
section: 4. Role: Method Lead (2 students)
text:
4. Role: Method Lead (2 students)
This week: Minjae (interviewing) and Seoyeon (coding & reliability)

What you are for
You are not summarizing the reading. You are explaining the logic of the method — what it assumes, where the researcher has to make a choice, and what the method licenses you to claim at the end. A classmate who missed the reading should leave able to use the method, not just name it.


Minjae — Method Lead 1: the interview as an instrument
Read closely: Kvale & Brinkmann Ch. 5–7.
Your 10 minutes should get at: - What kind of object an interview transcript is. Kvale & Brinkmann’s “miner vs. traveler” framing is the useful lever here: is the interview extracting knowledge that already sits inside the informant, or is it producing knowledge jointly in the conversation? These two positions lead to different interview guides and different claims. - The decision points a researcher actually faces: how structured, how many, when to stop, whether to send questions ahead, whether to record. - One thing people get wrong. Suggested: treating “number of interviews” as the quality signal, when the binding constraint is usually the quality of the guide and the researcher’s follow-up probes.
Bring a concrete artifact. Take one question from your own Horseshoe Wall entry and show the class two versions of an interview question that could address it — one leading, one not — and explain which follow-up probes you’d have ready. Two minutes of this is worth ten minutes of abstraction.


Seoyeon — Method Lead 2: from transcript to theme, and the reliability question
Read closely: Braun & Clarke (2006); Gioia et al. (2013); Saldaña Ch. 1–3; O’Connor & Joffe (2020).
Your 10 minutes should get at: - Braun & Clarke’s six phases, but the part worth your airtime is their insistence that themes do not “emerge” — the researcher constructs them. Explain why that matters for how you write a methods section. - The inductive/deductive and semantic/latent axes, with one CEM example of each. - The Gioia structure (1st-order informant terms → 2nd-order theoretical themes → aggregate dimensions) as a different answer to the same problem, and when you’d pick it over Braun & Clarke. - Then the hard one: O’Connor & Joffe. When does intercoder reliability make sense at all, and when is reporting a κ or α a ritual borrowed from a paradigm that doesn’t fit? How much of the corpus should be double-coded? Which coefficient, and why not percentage agreement?
Common failure mode: spending nine minutes on the six phases and thirty seconds on reliability. The reliability question is the one your classmates will need in the lab an hour later. Budget accordingly.


What you submit (Mon 9/28)
A 1-page Method Card. One page means one page. Template:
METHOD CARD — [method name]                        [your name] · Week 5

WHAT IT IS (2 sentences, no jargon)

CORE ASSUMPTIONS (3 bullets — what must be true for this to work)

DECISION POINTS (the 3–4 choices a researcher must make, and what
                 each choice costs)

WHAT IT LICENSES YOU TO CLAIM
WHAT IT DOES NOT LICENSE

MOST COMMON MISUSE IN CEM PAPERS

HORSESHOE BOX SERVED: ____________________
   (and one sentence on why)
The last line is not decoration. Every Method Card in this course ends by placing the method inside Fischer’s horseshoe. For Week 5 the honest answer is probably Research Tasks, but a good argument that thematic analysis can also reshape your Theoretical Limitation box would be more interesting.

title: Week 5 — How the seminar actually works
section: 5. Role: Exemplar Analyst (2 students)
text:
5. Role: Exemplar Analyst (2 students)
This week: Haneul (Spearing et al.) and Jiwon (Dossick & Neff)

What you are for
Reverse-engineer the paper. Not “what did they find” — how is the claim built, and what holds it up. You get 7 minutes and one slide.


The one slide
[Paper, one line]

RESEARCH QUESTION      →  as actually answered, not as stated in the abstract
DESIGN                 →  what kind of study is this
DATA                   →  who, how many, how long, collected how
ANALYSIS               →  what was done to the data, in what order
CLAIM                  →  the single sentence the paper is really asserting
WHAT HOLDS IT UP       →  the specific evidence for that sentence
LIMITS                 →  where the claim stops


Haneul — Spearing et al. (2022)
This is an unusual paper and that’s why it’s here: the authors apply more than one analysis technique to the same interview dataset (Arctic water and wastewater infrastructure in rural Alaska) and compare what each surfaces. Deductive content analysis produces frequency tables of pre-specified challenge categories; other passes surface challenges the researchers hadn’t anticipated.
Your job is to show the class exactly where the techniques diverged. Find a specific finding that one technique produced and another did not, and put it on the slide. That single concrete divergence is the whole point of assigning this paper.
Also: state clearly what the unit of analysis is. Is it the utility? The community? The excerpt? Papers like this are easy to misread on that point, and it determines what the frequency tables mean.


Jiwon — Dossick & Neff (2011)
Very different animal: ethnographic observation of BIM coordination meetings, building an argument that the technology’s structure does not dissolve the organizational divisions between trades — the productive work happens in informal, unstructured “messy talk” that clean technology tends to squeeze out.
Your job: - Reconstruct how they got from field observation to that argument. What counted as evidence? How many sites, how much time? - Be precise about the claim’s scope. Is this a claim about BIM, about these projects, or about the relationship between technological structure and organizational structure generally? - Read the 2010 JCEM paper as background. Same fieldwork, different argument. Put one line on your slide about how the same data supported two papers — that’s a genuinely useful thing for MS students to see.


What you submit (Mon 9/28)
The slide itself. That’s it — one slide, uploaded as PDF or image.
Common failure mode: producing a summary. If your slide could have been written after reading only the abstract and conclusion, you haven’t done the assignment. The Design/Data/Analysis rows are where the work is.

title: Week 5 — How the seminar actually works
section: 6. Role: Skeptic (2 students)
text:
6. Role: Skeptic (2 students)
This week: Taeyang (Spearing et al.) and Eunji (Dossick & Neff)

What you are for
Attack the paper’s validity — properly, in writing, on the form real reviewers use. You get 5 minutes to present the sharpest two points from your report.
The rule that matters: repeating a limitation the authors already stated in their own limitations section scores low. They already know. Your job is to find what they didn’t say.


Where to look, for these two papers
For a qualitative study, productive lines of attack usually run through: - Sampling and access. Who could have been interviewed but wasn’t, and would their absence change the conclusion? For Spearing et al., who in rural Alaskan water systems is structurally hard to reach? For Dossick & Neff, whose meetings were observed and whose weren’t? - The coding apparatus. Was a codebook developed before or after seeing the data? Was any of the corpus double-coded, and if so, is the reported agreement statistic the right one for that coding scheme? Read O’Connor & Joffe before you write this section — it will keep you from making the lazy version of this critique. - The inferential leap. Between a coded excerpt and a claimed theme there is a gap. Point at a specific place where you think the gap is too wide, and say what additional evidence would close it. - Rival explanations. Name one alternative account of the same data that the paper doesn’t rule out. - Transferability. Not “this is only one context” — that’s the lazy version. Instead: which specific feature of this context does the finding depend on, and what would have to be true elsewhere for it to travel?


What you submit (Mon 9/28)
A 1-page referee report on the ASCE reviewer form. Structure it like a real one:
SUMMARY OF THE PAPER (3 sentences, neutral — prove you read it fairly)

MAJOR CONCERNS (2–3, numbered, each with: what the problem is,
                why it threatens the conclusion, and what would fix it)

MINOR CONCERNS (2–3, brief)

RECOMMENDATION (accept / minor revision / major revision / reject)
                — and you must actually pick one
A worked fragment, so the register is clear:

Major concern 2. The codebook (Table 1) is presented as the analytical starting point, but the paper does not state whether it was derived from the literature before data collection or constructed after an initial pass through the transcripts. This matters because the frequency counts in Table 1 are used to support a claim about the relative prominence of challenge categories — and if the categories were drawn from the data, those frequencies are partly an artifact of the coding scheme rather than a finding about the sites. Suggested fix: state the provenance of the codebook explicitly, and if it was data-derived, either drop the comparative language or support it with a second, independently developed coding pass.

Note what that does: names the problem, links it to a specific claim, proposes a remedy. Three sentences. That’s the standard.
Common failure mode: hostility. A referee report is not a takedown. The tone that earns full marks is the tone of someone who wants the paper to get better.

title: Week 5 — How the seminar actually works
section: 7. Role: Discussant / Scribe (1 student)
text:
7. Role: Discussant / Scribe (1 student)
This week: Dohyun

Before class (Wed evening)
Read all nine entry tickets. Group them — you’ll usually find they cluster into three or four underlying questions even when nine different things were asked. Pick two to open with, and email the instructor which two by Wednesday night so the framing segment can set them up.
Choose for productivity, not politeness. The best opening question is one where two readings of the week genuinely disagree.


During class (25 minutes)
You are chairing, not presenting. Practically: - Open with your first chosen ticket, addressed to a specific person — “Seoyeon, you argued X in your Method Card; this ticket says the opposite. Take it.” - Track who has spoken. In a 16-person room, four people will take 80% of the airtime unless someone stops it. Stopping it is your job. - When the discussion loops, say so and move to the second question. - Reserve the last three minutes to ask the room: what did we not resolve? That unresolved thing goes in your synthesis.


After class (by Sat 10/3, 18:00)
A 300-word synthesis posted to the course site. Not minutes. Structure: 1. The question the room actually spent its time on (often not the one on the syllabus) 2. The two strongest opposing positions, stated fairly 3. What remained unresolved 4. One sentence: what this changes about how you’d design a qualitative study
These accumulate. By December the class will have built its own methods notebook out of thirteen of these.

title: Week 5 — How the seminar actually works
section: 8. If you don’t have a role this week (nine of you)
text:
8. If you don’t have a role this week (nine of you)
Entry ticket, due Wed 9/30 18:00. One question, 2–3 sentences.
The bar: your question should be answerable only by someone who did the reading, and it should not have a settled answer.
Weak: > What is thematic analysis?
Also weak (a comment, not a question): > I found Braun and Clarke very useful and I agree that themes are constructed.
Strong: > Braun & Clarke insist themes are constructed by the researcher, not discovered. Spearing et al. report frequency counts of coded categories. Are those two positions compatible — can you count something you constructed and still call the count evidence?
Strong: > O’Connor & Joffe argue intercoder reliability is only appropriate under certain conditions. Dossick & Neff report ethnographic observation with no reliability statistic at all. Is that a gap in the paper, or is a reliability statistic simply the wrong instrument for what they were doing?
Strong: > Dossick & Neff got two papers with different arguments out of one body of fieldwork. At what point does that become double-dipping rather than legitimate secondary analysis?
Both of the first two examples above happen to also work as opening questions — which is what the Discussant is looking for.

title: Week 5 — How the seminar actually works
section: 9. Lab 2 (40 min in class, deliverable due 10/8)
text:
9. Lab 2 (40 min in class, deliverable due 10/8)
Everyone, in pairs.

(15 min) You’ll receive the same anonymized construction interview transcript and a shared six-code codebook. Code it independently — no talking to your partner yet.
(10 min) Compute pairwise Krippendorff’s α against your partner. R: irr::kripp.alpha(). Python: krippendorff.alpha(). Both will be pre-installed on the lab machines; a starter script is on the course site.
(15 min) Half the room (assigned in class) re-codes with LLM assistance. Compare: does α go up? Does code granularity change? What disappears?

Deliverable (2–3 pages, due 10/8): - Coding memo — where you and your partner diverged, and why - Reliability table — α per code, not just overall - One page: where human and LLM-assisted coding diverged, and what that implies for whether an LLM can be a “second coder” at all
The interesting result is usually not the α value. It’s the argument you and your partner have in step 2 about why one of you coded an excerpt as resource constraint and the other as institutional barrier. Write that argument down — it’s the actual finding.

text:
11. One thing to keep in mind this week
Week 5 is the first week where the method you’re studying might actually be the method you use. When you leave, go update your Horseshoe Wall entry. If thematic analysis or a Gioia-style structure could fill your Research Tasks box, say so and say what data you’d need. title: Weekly schedule
section: Week 2 (9/10) — History of CEM research
text:
Week 2 (9/10) — History of CEM research
Focus: How the field’s standards of evidence were built, and why the current track list looks the way it does
Instructor segment (25 min): the four-era arc — 1955–75 (emergence: Peurifoy, Fondahl’s precedence diagramming, Oglesby & Parker’s operations analysis, Gates/Carr bidding debate, Halpin’s CYCLONE), 1975–95 (institutionalization: JCEM, CRC, CII, CIFE; Ashley on risk sharing; Tatum on innovation; Howell/Tommelein/Ballard on lean; Levitt on organizational design; expert systems, neural nets, GAs), 1995–2005 (Peña-Mora on collaboration technology; sensors, RFID, GPS; Fischer’s 4D CAD; Martinez & Kamat simulation; Hendrickson & Horvath EIO-LCA), 2005–present (reality capture, automation, and the turn toward social science).
Student workshop (4 teams × 4): each team takes one era and two landmark works from it. The presentation question is not “what did they find” but “what counted as a legitimate method then, what data existed, and what got it published?” Each team closes by mapping current CRC / i3CE track names onto their era.
Readings - Levitt, R. E. (2007). “CEM research for the next 50 years: Maximizing economic, environmental, and societal value of the built environment.” JCEM, 133(9), 619–628. [Peurifoy Award Lecture] - Taylor, J. E., & Jaselskis, E. J. (2010). “Introduction to the special issue on research methodologies in CEM.” JCEM, 136(1), 1–2. - Jahren, C. T., et al. (2023). “Second special collection on research methodologies in CEM.” JCEM, 149(2). - CRC and i3CE current track listings (2 pp., handout).
→ If you only have time for one: Levitt (2007). It’s short, it’s the field talking about itself, and every team will need it regardless of which era they draw.
Lab (method archaeology): each student is assigned one JCEM volume — half from the 1980s–90s, half from the last three years — and codes its table of contents using the §3 taxonomy. The class assembles a shared method-frequency chart across eras.
Assignment for W3: read Fischer (2006) and reconstruct the horseshoe for the paper assigned in W1.

title: Weekly schedule
section: Week 3 (9/17) — Formalizing construction knowledge: the CIFE horseshoe
text:
Week 3 (9/17) — Formalizing construction knowledge: the CIFE horseshoe
Focus: The field’s own research process model — and the framework the rest of this course fills in
Instructor segment (25 min): the seven boxes — Observed Problem in Practice → Theoretical Limitation → Research Questions → Research Tasks → Research Results → Contribution to Knowledge → Practical Significance, with Intuition running underneath. Worked through with the Disney California Adventure lagoon / 4D modeling example (Akbas 2003). Two things Fischer insists on: the problem statement must be specific enough that success criteria are visible, and the maximum anxiety principle — always advance the step with the greatest uncertainty first.
Studio (the core of the week): present the horseshoe you reconstructed for your assigned paper. Pairs then debate one question — which box is that paper weakest at? Most CEM papers collapse the Theoretical Limitation and Contribution to Knowledge boxes and jump from problem straight to tasks.
Fischer’s four test methods, mapped onto this course:







Fischer’s test method
Where this course teaches it




Variation studies on retrospective cases
W10 (archival identification), W12 (simulation experiments)


Expert panel review
W7 (Delphi and structured elicitation)


Charrette test
W10 (controlled experiment design), W11 (XR-enabled charrettes)


Prospective / intervention case study
W6 (case study design), W10 (multiple-baseline field designs), W14 (action research)



Readings - Fischer, M. (2006). “Formalizing construction knowledge for concurrent performance-based design.” Proc. 13th EG-ICE Workshop, Ascona, Switzerland. (Springer LNCS 4200.) - Van de Ven, A. H. (1989). “Nothing is quite so practical as a good theory.” AMR, 14(4), 486–489. - Clayton, M. J., Kunz, J. C., & Fischer, M. A. (1998). The Charrette Test Method. CIFE Technical Report #120, Stanford University. - Hevner, A. R., March, S. T., Park, J., & Ram, S. (2004). “Design science in information systems research.” MIS Quarterly, 28(1), 75–105. §1–2 only — for comparison in W14. - Reference: Akbas, R. (2003). Geometry Based Modeling and Simulation of Construction Processes. PhD thesis, Stanford University.
→ If you only have time for one: Fischer (2006) itself. Everything else this week supports it.
⚠️ A limit worth knowing now. The horseshoe grew out of CIFE/VDC work and fits artifact-producing research beautifully. It fits interpretive and purely descriptive research much less well — if you’re running an interview study, you’ll struggle to fill Practical Significance honestly. Keep this in mind; Week 6 introduces a contrasting map (Eisenhardt’s inductive process model) for exactly this reason.
A worked local example. Alongside Fischer’s Disney-lagoon case, we’ll trace one research line from this department all the way around the horseshoe: deictic gesture-based spatial referencing for human–robot collaboration. Observed problem (site instructions to robots are improvised and imprecise) → theoretical limitation (gesture-based HRI evaluated only in small, controlled spaces) → question → tasks → results → contribution → practical significance. The published endpoint is Yoon, Kim, Park & Ahn (2023), JCEM, 149(7), which returns as an exemplar in Week 11. Seeing a full horseshoe from a project you could walk down the hall and ask about makes the abstract boxes concrete.
Assignment (ongoing): build the horseshoe for your own research idea. Post it to the Horseshoe Wall — it’s revised weekly from here and becomes the W7 pre-proposal.

text:
Week 6 (10/8) — Qualitative II: case study, ethnography, and mixed methods
Focus: Case selection, embedded units, replication logic, trustworthiness; combining strands
Methods readings - Yin, R. K. (2018). Case Study Research and Applications (6th ed.). SAGE. Ch. 2–4. - Eisenhardt, K. M. (1989). “Building theories from case study research.” AMR, 14(4), 532–550. [The promised contrast to the horseshoe — see the discussion prompt below] - Eisenhardt, K. M., & Graebner, M. E. (2007). “Theory building from cases: Opportunities and challenges.” AMJ, 50(1), 25–32. - Flyvbjerg, B. (2006). “Five misunderstandings about case-study research.” Qualitative Inquiry, 12(2), 219–245. - Lincoln, Y. S., & Guba, E. G. (1985). Naturalistic Inquiry. SAGE. Ch. 11 (trustworthiness) only. - Creswell, J. W., & Plano Clark, V. L. (2018). Designing and Conducting Mixed Methods Research (3rd ed.). SAGE. Ch. 3.
→ If you only have time for one: Eisenhardt (1989). It’s short, it’s concrete, and it’s the reading the discussion prompt is built around.
CEM exemplars - Taylor, J. E. (2007). “Antecedents of successful three-dimensional computer-aided design implementation in design and construction networks.” JCEM, 133(12), 993–1002. [Case study exemplar] - Ham, N., Moon, S., Kim, J.-H., & Kim, J.-J. (2018). “Economic analysis of design errors in BIM-based high-rise construction projects: Case study of Haeundae L project.” JCEM, 144(6), 05018006. On mixed methods specifically: a clean, single-paper CEM exemplar that is unambiguously “mixed methods done well” is genuinely hard to find — it’s an underused design in this field. Revisit Spearing et al. (2022, Week 5) through a mixed-methods lens: it applies three qualitative techniques to one dataset, which is adjacent to but not the same as integrating qualitative and quantitative strands. Treat the absence of a tidy exemplar here as data about the field, and flag it in your own proposal if you’re the one attempting a genuine mixed-methods design.

CEM readings and exemplars - Zhang, et al. (2022). “Mitigating common method bias in construction engineering and management research.” JCEM, 148(9). DOI: 10.1061/(ASCE)CO.1943-7862.0002364. [Finds ~90% of survey-based JCEM papers likely affected. This is a review/discussion piece, not itself a substantive exemplar — read it for the diagnosis, not as a model to imitate.] - Hallowell, M. R., & Gambatese, J. A. (2010). “Qualitative research: Application of the Delphi method to CEM research.” JCEM, 136(1), 99–107. [CEM methods reading — a how-to essay, not an exemplar.] - Hallowell, M. R., & Gambatese, J. A. (2009). “Activity-based safety risk quantification for concrete formwork construction.” JCEM, 135(10), 990–998. [Delphi exemplar] - Fang, D., Chen, Y., & Wong, L. (2006). “Safety climate in construction industry: A case study in Hong Kong.” JCEM, 132(6), 573–584. [Survey exemplar]
Lab 4 (graded): (a) Draft a 10-item instrument for one construct from your own pre-proposal; run a 15-minute cognitive pretest on a classmate and revise. (b) On the provided dataset, run Harman’s single-factor test and a marker-variable test, then argue whether CMB is a real threat or a ritual in that case.

title: Weekly schedule
section: Week 8 (10/22) — Pre-proposal presentations, peer review, and journal fit
text:
Week 8 (10/22) — Pre-proposal presentations, peer review, and journal fit
No new readings.

Present the pre-proposal in 6 minutes + 4 minutes Q&A — problem, gap, question, proposed design, why that design. The horseshoe is the required slide format.
You’re assigned two peers’ pre-proposals and write a referee report using the ASCE reviewer form and the COPE Ethical Guidelines for Peer Reviewers (2017).
Reports are returned anonymously; write a one-page response-to-reviewers letter (due W10).
Journal fit clinic: name a target journal and justify the fit against its aims, typical methods, and recent volumes.

title: Weekly schedule
section: Week 9 (10/29) — Quantitative modeling and reporting
text:
Week 9 (10/29) — Quantitative modeling and reporting
Focus: Regression; SEM (covariance-based and PLS); reporting standards; effect sizes over p-values
Methods readings - Wooldridge, J. M. (2019). Introductory Econometrics (7th ed.). Cengage. Ch. 3–4 (skim), Ch. 9 (specification). - Kline, R. B. (2023). Principles and Practice of Structural Equation Modeling (5th ed.). Guilford. Ch. 1–3, 9. - Hair, J. F., Hult, G. T. M., Ringle, C. M., & Sarstedt, M. (2022). A Primer on PLS-SEM (3rd ed.). SAGE. Ch. 1–2, 6. - Rönkkö, M., & Cho, E. (2022). “An updated guideline for assessing discriminant validity.” ORM, 25(1), 6–14. - Cumming, G. (2014). “The new statistics: Why and how.” Psychological Science, 25(1), 7–29.
→ If you only have time for one: Kline, Ch. 1–3. It’s the conceptual foundation for the SEM half of this week’s lab, and Hair et al. only makes sense once Kline’s basics are in place.
CEM exemplars - Molenaar, K., Washington, S., & Diekmann, J. (2000). “Structural equation model of construction contract dispute potential.” JCEM, 126(4), 268–277. [SEM exemplar] - Doloi, H. (2013). “Cost overruns and failure in project management: Understanding the roles of key stakeholders in construction projects.” JCEM, 139(3), 267–279. [Regression exemplar — factor analysis plus multivariate regression on survey data]
CEM methods reading (discussion piece, not an exemplar): “Methodological consistency for quantitative analysis and reporting in project delivery system performance research.” JCEM (Second Special Collection, 2022).
Lab 5 (graded): On one provided dataset, fit (i) OLS with a mediator tested by regression and (ii) a PLS-SEM model of the same theory. Deliverable: 2-page memo — “Would a reviewer accept both? Which would you defend, and on what grounds?”

title: Weekly schedule
section: Week 10 (11/5) — Causal inference: experiments, quasi-experiments, and archival identification
text:
Week 10 (11/5) — Causal inference: experiments, quasi-experiments, and archival identification
Focus: Internal validity; randomization; single-case and multiple-baseline designs; DiD / IV / matching; preregistration Fischer’s “variation studies on retrospective cases” and “charrette test” get their formal treatment here 📌 Response-to-reviewers letters from Week 8 due
Methods readings - Shadish, W. R., Cook, T. D., & Campbell, D. T. (2002). Experimental and Quasi-Experimental Designs for Generalized Causal Inference. Houghton Mifflin. Ch. 1–3. - Angrist, J. D., & Pischke, J.-S. (2015). Mastering ’Metrics. Princeton UP. Ch. 1, 5. - Cunningham, S. (2021). Causal Inference: The Mixtape. Yale UP. [Open access] Ch. on DiD. - Kazdin, A. E. (2011). Single-Case Research Designs (2nd ed.). Oxford UP. Ch. 5–6. - Nosek, B. A., Ebersole, C. R., DeHaven, A. C., & Mellor, D. T. (2018). “The preregistration revolution.” PNAS, 115(11), 2600–2606. - Simmons, J. P., Nelson, L. D., & Simonsohn, U. (2011). “False-positive psychology.” Psychological Science, 22(11), 1359–1366.
→ If you only have time for one: Shadish, Cook & Campbell, Ch. 1–3. It’s the reading Lab 6 is directly built on.
CEM exemplars - Albert, A., Hallowell, M. R., Lingard, H., & Kleiner, B. M. (2015). “Multiple baseline testing: Experimental method for drawing causal inferences in CEM research.” JCEM, 141(7), 04015012. [The right answer to “we can’t randomize on a construction site”] - Hasanzadeh, S., Esmaeili, B., & Dodd, M. D. (2017). “Measuring the impacts of safety knowledge on construction workers’ attentional allocation and hazard detection using remote eye-tracking technology.” JME, 33(5), 04017024. [Experiment exemplar] - Flyvbjerg, B., Holm, M. K. S., & Buhl, S. (2002). “Underestimating costs in public works projects: Error or lie?” JAPA, 68(3), 279–295. [Archival exemplar]
CEM methods reading (guidance piece, not an exemplar): Lucko, G., & Mitchell, Z. (2010). “Quantitative research: Preparation of incongruous economic data sets for archival data analysis.” JCEM, 136(1), 49–57.
Lab 6 (graded): Take one intervention relevant to your own horseshoe and design three studies for it — a lab experiment, a multiple-baseline field design, and a quasi-experimental archival design. Run a power analysis for the first. Write the preregistration for whichever you would actually run.

title: Weekly schedule
section: Week 11 (11/12) — Instrumented human-subject research: sensing, eye-tracking, and XR
text:
Week 11 (11/12) — Instrumented human-subject research: sensing, eye-tracking, and XR
Focus: Physiological and behavioral measurement; ecological validity; XR as a research instrument, not a demo 📌 Horseshoe Wall checkpoint — second graded review of your horseshoe
Methods readings - Li, N., Du, J., González, V. A., & Chen, J. (2022). “Methodology for extended reality–enabled experimental research in construction engineering and management.” JCEM, 148(10), 04022106. DOI: 10.1061/(ASCE)CO.1943-7862.0002367. - Cacioppo, J. T., Tassinary, L. G., & Berntson, G. G. (Eds.) (2016). Handbook of Psychophysiology (4th ed.). Cambridge UP. Ch. 1 — inference from physiological signals to psychological constructs, the key conceptual problem. - Slater, M., & Sanchez-Vives, M. V. (2016). “Enhancing our lives with immersive virtual reality.” Frontiers in Robotics and AI, 3, 74.
→ If you only have time for one: Cacioppo, Tassinary & Berntson, Ch. 1. Every wearable-sensor and eye-tracking study lives or dies on the inferential gap this chapter names, and it’s the harder-to-find idea of the three.
CEM exemplars - Yoon, S., Kim, Y., Park, M., & Ahn, C. R. (2023). “Effects of spatial characteristics on the human–robot communication using deictic gesture in construction.” JCEM, 149(7), 04023049. DOI: 10.1061/JCEMD4.COENG-12997. [Controlled human-subject experiment exemplar — and the same line of work you saw framed as a horseshoe in Week 3. Read it asking: how did the wall/ceiling workspace conditions get chosen, and what does that choice buy and cost in external validity?] - Yang, K., Ahn, C. R., Vuran, M. C., & Aria, S. S. (2016). “Semi-supervised near-miss fall detection for ironworkers with a wearable inertial measurement unit.” Automation in Construction, 68, 194–202. [Wearable IMU exemplar — real ironworkers, real site, and an honest treatment of what 75.9% recall does and doesn’t license] - Jebelli, H., Choi, B., & Lee, S. (2019). “Application of wearable biosensors to construction sites. I: Assessing workers’ stress.” JCEM, 145(12), 04019079. [Physiological sensing exemplar] - Golparvar-Fard, M., Peña-Mora, F., & Savarese, S. (2011). “Integrated sequential as-built and as-planned representation with D4AR tools in support of decision-making tasks in the AEC/FM industry.” JCEM, 137(12), 1099–1116. [Reality-capture / computer-vision exemplar] - For the lab specifically: Yang, K., Ahn, C. R., & Kim, H. (2019). “Validating ambulatory gait assessment technique for hazard sensing in construction environments.” Automation in Construction, 98, 302–309. [A validation study rather than a system paper — the closest published model for the measurement-validity memo you’ll write below]
CEM methods readings (review/discussion, not exemplars): Ahn, C. R., Lee, S., Sun, C., Jebelli, H., Yang, K., & Choi, B. (2019). “Wearable sensing technology applications in construction safety and health.” JCEM, 145(11), 03119007. · Bogus, S. M., Lippitt, C. D., et al. (2022). “Implementing remote-sensing methodologies for construction research: An unoccupied airborne system perspective.” JCEM (Second Special Collection).
Lab 7 (in-class): If equipment is available, run a 20-minute in-class data collection (HR/EDA wristband or webcam eye-tracker) on a simple attention task, then examine the raw signal together. The pedagogical point is how far the raw trace sits from the construct. Deliverable: measurement-validity memo — signal → feature → construct → what else could produce that signal.

title: Weekly schedule
section: Week 12 (11/19) — Simulation as a research method
text:
Week 12 (11/19) — Simulation as a research method
Focus: DES, system dynamics, ABM; the verification and validation problem
Methods readings - Sargent, R. G. (2013). “Verification and validation of simulation models.” Journal of Simulation, 7, 12–24. - Sterman, J. D. (2000). Business Dynamics. McGraw-Hill. Ch. 1, 21 (model validity). - Railsback, S. F., & Grimm, V. (2019). Agent-Based and Individual-Based Modeling (2nd ed.). Princeton UP. Ch. 1–3. - Grimm, V., et al. (2020). “The ODD protocol for describing agent-based and other simulation models: A second update.” JASSS, 23(2), 7.
→ If you only have time for one: Sargent (2013). V&V is the part of simulation research everyone skips and every reviewer checks — it’s the reading Lab 8 is built around.
CEM exemplars - Larsson, J., Lu, W., Krantz, J., & Olofsson, T. (2016). “Discrete event simulation analysis of product and process platforms: A bridge construction case study.” JCEM, 142(4), 04015097. [DES exemplar] - Peña-Mora, F., & Park, M. (2001). “Dynamic planning for fast-tracking building construction projects.” JCEM, 127(6), 445–456. [SD exemplar — the feedback structure of fast-tracking, modeled explicitly. Note that this paper drew a published Discussion from Greg Howell and a reply; read both if you want to see how modeling assumptions get contested in print, which is rarer and more instructive than it should be.] - Jung, M., Park, M., Lee, H.-S., & Chi, S. (2017). “Agent-based lift system simulation model for high-rise building construction projects.” Journal of Computing in Civil Engineering, 31(6). DOI: 10.1061/(ASCE)CP.1943-5487.0000707. [ABM exemplar — a good contrast with Watkins et al. on what counts as an “agent”] - Watkins, M., Mukherjee, A., Onder, N., & Mattila, K. (2009). “Using agent-based modeling to study construction labor productivity as an emergent property of individual and crew interactions.” JCEM, 135(7), 657–667. [ABM exemplar] - Lyneis, J. M., & Ford, D. N. (2007). “System dynamics applied to project management.” System Dynamics Review, 23(2–3), 157–189 · Love, P. E. D., Holt, G. D., Shen, L. Y., Li, H., & Irani, Z. (2002). “Using systems dynamics to better understand change and rework in construction project management systems.” IJPM, 20(6), 425–436. [Further SD exemplars]
CEM methods reading (discussion, not an exemplar): AbouRizk, S. (2010). “Role of simulation in construction engineering and management.” JCEM, 136(10), 1140–1153. [Useful history — trace the line back to Halpin’s CYCLONE from Week 2 — but it’s a field overview, not a single study.] · “Methodology for conducting discrete-event simulation studies in construction engineering and management.” JCEM (Second Special Collection, 2022).
Lab 8 (in-class): Given a small provided model (SimPy DES or NetLogo ABM), (a) write its ODD description, (b) design a validation plan, (c) identify one parameter whose uncertainty would change the paper’s conclusion. Deliverable: V&V memo.

title: Weekly schedule
section: Week 13 (11/26) — Data-driven research: ML, computer vision, NLP
text:
Week 13 (11/26) — Data-driven research: ML, computer vision, NLP
Focus: Prediction vs. explanation; leakage; generalization across subjects and sites; reproducibility
Methods readings - Shmueli, G. (2010). “To explain or to predict?” Statistical Science, 25(3), 289–310. - Kapoor, S., & Narayanan, A. (2023). “Leakage and the reproducibility crisis in machine-learning-based science.” Patterns, 4(9), 100804. - James, G., Witten, D., Hastie, T., & Tibshirani, R. (2021). An Introduction to Statistical Learning (2nd ed.). Springer. Ch. 5 (resampling). - Pineau, J., et al. (2021). “Improving reproducibility in machine learning research.” JMLR, 22(164).
→ If you only have time for one: Shmueli (2010) — assign it to everyone, not only the computational students. It’s the reading that reframes every ML paper you’ll read afterward.
CEM exemplars - Fang, Q., Li, H., Luo, X., Ding, L., Luo, H., Rose, T. M., & An, W. (2018). “Detecting non-hardhat-use by a deep learning method from far-field surveillance videos.” Automation in Construction, 85, 1–9. [CV exemplar] - Zhang, J., & El-Gohary, N. M. (2016). “Semantic NLP-based information extraction from construction regulatory documents for automated compliance checking.” JCEM, 142(3), 04015014. [NLP exemplar] - Tixier, A. J.-P., Hallowell, M. R., Rajagopalan, B., & Bowman, D. (2016). “Application of machine learning to construction injury prediction.” Automation in Construction, 69, 102–114. [Prediction exemplar] - Kim, J., Chi, S., & Ahn, C. R. (2021). “Hybrid kinematic–visual sensing approach for activity recognition of construction equipment.” Journal of Building Engineering, 44, 102709. [Sensor-fusion exemplar — read it against Kapoor & Narayanan: what would subject-wise or site-wise held-out testing have shown here, and was it done?]
CEM methods reading (discussion, not an exemplar): “Importance of testing with independent subjects and contexts for machine-learning models to monitor construction workers’ psychophysiological responses.” JCEM (Second Special Collection, 2022). [Pairs directly with Kapoor & Narayanan — read for the diagnosis, not as a model paper.]
Short RL segment: the reinforcement-learning review in the Second Special Collection, for anyone whose proposal involves sequential decisions.
Lab 9 (graded): Given a small provided dataset with a deliberately planted leakage problem, reproduce the “published” accuracy, find the leak, and re-evaluate under subject-wise cross-validation. Deliverable: a one-page correction note in the style of a journal comment.

title: Weekly schedule
section: Week 14 (12/3) — Closing the horseshoe: design science, action research, optimization, and validation
text:
Week 14 (12/3) — Closing the horseshoe: design science, action research, optimization, and validation
Focus: When the contribution is a method, tool, or framework — how to make that a defensible research claim, and how far it generalizes 📌 Final proposal due (8–10 pages) at the end of this week
Methods readings - Hevner, A. R., March, S. T., Park, J., & Ram, S. (2004). “Design science in information systems research.” MIS Quarterly, 28(1), 75–105. Full paper now (§1–2 were read in W3). - Peffers, K., Tuunanen, T., Rothenberger, M. A., & Chatterjee, S. (2007). “A design science research methodology for information systems research.” JMIS, 24(3), 45–77. - Sein, M. K., Henfridsson, O., Purao, S., Rossi, M., & Lindgren, R. (2011). “Action design research.” MIS Quarterly, 35(1), 37–56. - Coughlan, P., & Coghlan, D. (2002). “Action research for operations management.” IJOPM, 22(2), 220–240. - Deb, K., Pratap, A., Agarwal, S., & Meyarivan, T. (2002). “A fast and elitist multiobjective genetic algorithm: NSGA-II.” IEEE Trans. Evolutionary Computation, 6(2), 182–197. - Bem, D. J. (2004). “Writing the empirical journal article.” In J. M. Darley et al. (Eds.), The Compleat Academic. APA.
→ If you only have time for one: Hevner et al. (2004), full paper. This is the week that revisits your Week 3 horseshoe against a rival framework, and Hevner is that rival.
CEM exemplars - El-Rayes, K., & Kandil, A. (2005). “Time-cost-quality trade-off analysis for highway construction.” JCEM, 131(4), 477–486. [Optimization exemplar] - Eriksson, P. E. (2010). “Improving construction supply chain collaboration and performance: A lean construction pilot project.” Supply Chain Management: An International Journal, 15(5), 394–403. [Action research exemplar — explicitly uses an action research design in a real lean-construction pilot] - DSR exemplar: revisit Fischer’s own Akbas/Disney-lagoon case from Week 3. You already reconstructed its horseshoe; now evaluate it against Hevner’s design-science criteria instead.
CEM methods readings (position/discussion papers, not exemplars): Azhar, S., Ahmad, I., & Sein, M. K. (2010). “Action research as a proactive research method for construction engineering and management.” JCEM, 136(1), 87–98. · Lucko, G., & Rojas, E. M. (2010). “Research validation: Challenges and opportunities in the construction domain.” JCEM, 136(1), 127–135. · O’Brien, W. J., Thomas, S. R., et al. (2022). “Recommended practices for effective management of academia–industry collaborative research teams in construction management.” JCEM (Second Special Collection). · “Optimization research: Enhancing the robustness of large-scale multiobjective optimization in construction.” JCEM (Second Special Collection, 2022).
Closing discussion (the bookend to Week 3). Put Fischer’s horseshoe and Hevner’s DSR framework side by side. A large share of CEM papers propose a framework or system and “validate” it on one case. Is that the horseshoe done implicitly and badly, or a legitimate mode with different standards? Then: has your own horseshoe survived the semester intact, and if not, which box broke first?
Lab 10 (in-class): Take any framework-type paper the class picks and rewrite its contribution statement and evaluation section as a rigorous DSR study. What additional evidence would be required?
Role-play: one student pitches their study to a contractor; another plays the contractor deciding whether to grant site access.

title: Weekly schedule
section: Week 15 (12/10) — Final proposal defense (mock review panel)
text:
Week 15 (12/10) — Final proposal defense (mock review panel)
Present for 8 minutes and take 7 minutes of questions from a three-person panel of classmates plus the instructor, using the ASCE review criteria. Panel members submit scored review forms; the instructor moderates.
Close the loop twice: the Week 1 interest cards come back, and the Week 3 horseshoe sits beside the final one. What changed, and why?
Course ends here.
